subject: mathematics
question_text: By using the matrix inversion method, solve 2x − y + 3z = 9, x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2.

mark_split.label: Write the system as AX = D and X = A⁻¹D
Find det A and check it is not zero
Transpose to Adj A and write A⁻¹
Multiply A⁻¹ by D and state the solution

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.29 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 19.1, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: TS 19 · AP 15. THE 4+3 SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S, though not in its usual form: no [N Marks] tags are printed against these answers, but a margin note on book p.30 states it in words — "Just finding A⁻¹ gives u 4 Marks. For remaining steps u get 3 Marks!". The five steps here honour that exactly: det A, the cofactor matrix and the adjoint/inverse total 4, and the matrix form plus the multiplication total 3. The finer 1/2/1 and 1/2 division INSIDE each half is ours, not the book's. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all three matrix-inversion answers in this unit, deliberately: the three questions are one method over different numbers. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Find the cofactor matrix" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by the matrix inversion method — say what you have to find first, how you build the inverse, and what you multiply at the end.

steps.label: Write it as AX = D
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the plan as well as the matrices: the solution of AX = D is X = A⁻¹D, so everything after this line is about building A⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: X = A⁻¹D is the plan — write it down before building anything.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}

lines: The solution of AX = D is X = A⁻¹D.

recall.must_convey: That the system is written as AX = D and that its solution is X = A⁻¹D — so the inverse is what has to be found.
accept: write it as A X equals D so the solution is X equals A inverse D
put the system in matrix form and then X is A inverse times D
form A X and D and say the solution is A inverse into D
AX equals D form lo rasi, solution X equals A inverse D ani rasta
the coefficient matrix times the unknowns equals the constants so multiply by the inverse

steps.why: AX = D is solved by multiplying both sides on the LEFT by A⁻¹. Writing X = A⁻¹D at the start states the plan, and the plan is what the remaining marks pay for.
common_mistakes: Writing X = DA⁻¹; matrix multiplication does not commute, and that order does not even have matching sizes.
Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.
Missing a coefficient of 1 or −1 written with no number in front.

steps.label: Find det A
steps.margin_note: Second mark. det A is −2. It has to be non-zero or A has no inverse at all and this method cannot start — so write the check, do not just compute the number.
steps.memory_tip: det A = −2, and it must be non-zero or A has no inverse at all. Write the check.

recall.must_convey: That det A is computed, comes to −2, and that being non-zero is what guarantees A⁻¹ exists.
accept: find the determinant of A which is minus 2 and since it is not zero the inverse exists
compute det A and check it is non zero so A is non singular
expand the determinant of the coefficient matrix, it is not zero so the inverse exists
det A kanukoni, zero kaadu kabatti inverse untundi
the determinant must be non zero for A inverse to exist

steps.why: A⁻¹ is Adj A divided by det A. A zero determinant would mean dividing by zero — which is exactly why a singular matrix has no inverse and this method would stop here.
common_mistakes: Computing det A but never writing that it is non-zero.
Getting the sign pattern wrong: plus, minus, plus along the top row.
Confusing det A with the trace or with the sum of a row.

steps.label: Find the cofactor matrix
steps.margin_note: Three marks, and the longest part of the question — nine 2×2 determinants. The sign board is + − + / − + − / + − +. Cross out the entry’s own row and column, take the determinant of what is left, then apply that sign.
steps.memory_tip: Nine 2×2 determinants with the + − + / − + − / + − + sign board.
lines: Delete each entry’s row and column, take the 2×2
determinant, and apply the sign board + − + / − + − / + − +:

recall.must_convey: That each cofactor is the 2×2 determinant left after deleting that entry’s row and column, with the alternating plus-minus sign applied.
accept: for each entry delete its row and column take the two by two determinant and put the plus minus sign
find the nine cofactors using the minors with the alternating sign pattern
cross out the row and column of each entry and take the determinant of what is left with the correct sign
prathi entry ki row column teesesi, two by two determinant teeskoni sign pettali
build the cofactor matrix from the nine minors with signs plus minus plus

steps.why: A minor is just the smaller determinant. A cofactor is that minor with a sign attached, and the sign depends only on the position — which is why the board is worth memorising once rather than deriving nine times.
common_mistakes: Writing the minors and forgetting the sign board entirely.
Applying the signs to the wrong positions; the corners are all plus.
Deleting the wrong row or column for the off-diagonal entries.

steps.label: Transpose to get Adj A
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark, and the step most often skipped. Adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix — rows become columns. Then A⁻¹ is Adj A divided by det A.
steps.memory_tip: Adj A is the cofactor matrix TRANSPOSED, then divided by det A.
lines: Adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix:

recall.must_convey: That the adjoint is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix, and that A⁻¹ is the adjoint divided by det A.
accept: take the transpose of the cofactor matrix to get adj A then divide by det A to get the inverse
adjoint is the transpose of the cofactors and A inverse is adj A over det A
transpose the cofactor matrix and divide by the determinant
cofactor matrix transpose teeste adj A vasthundi, det A tho divide cheste inverse
A inverse equals one by det A times the adjoint

steps.why: Forgetting the transpose gives a matrix that looks right and is wrong, and nothing later in the question will reveal it. On a symmetric cofactor matrix the transpose changes nothing — which is exactly why the habit has to be written down every time.
common_mistakes: Using the cofactor matrix directly as the adjoint without transposing.
Dividing only one row by det A instead of the whole matrix.
Multiplying by det A instead of dividing.

steps.label: Multiply A⁻¹ by D
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Multiply row by column, then divide every entry by det A. Here det A is −2 and all three products are negative, so all three answers come out positive.
steps.memory_tip: det A is −2 and all three products are negative, so all three answers come out positive.
lines: X = A⁻¹D. Multiplying row by column:

recall.must_convey: That A⁻¹ is multiplied by D row against column, and that dividing by det A gives x = 1, y = 2, z = 3.
accept: multiply A inverse by D row into column and divide by det A to get the three values
do the matrix multiplication and then divide each entry by the determinant
X equals A inverse D so multiply out and read off x y and z
A inverse ni D tho multiply chesi det A tho divide cheste x y z vasthai
row into column multiplication gives the column matrix and that is the solution

steps.why: X comes out as a single column matrix, and its three entries ARE x, y and z in that order. Reading them off in the wrong order is the last thing that can go wrong.
common_mistakes: Multiplying column by row instead of row by column.
Dividing by det A only once instead of on every entry.
Never substituting back to check — x=1, y=2, z=3 in the first equation gives 2−2+9 = 9.

insider_note: The same system as the Cramer and Gauss-Jordan versions, but the method asked for is the inverse: X = A⁻¹D. Multiply in that order — D A⁻¹ is not even defined.
